name: Dutch
intro: The main model is Netherlands standard Dutch, with Belgian usage acknowledged as a separate important exposure area. Learn de/het nouns with plurals and pronunciation. Dutch /ɣ/-type sounds vary geographically; do not treat one harsh sound as a national accent requirement. Professional comprehension needs embedded-clause processing and conventional phrasing.

foundation.name: Dutch
notes: Dutch uses 26 letters. ij is an important digraph, often capitalised together at the start: IJssel. It is not an additional letter in standard alphabetical ordering. Letter names differ from sounds in words.

Compare man and maan. A single vowel in an open syllable can be long: ma-ken. A doubled consonant keeps the preceding vowel short: man-nen. oe is /u/; ie is /i/; eu and ui need listening practice; English spellings are poor substitutes.

g and ch are often fricatives, with softer regional realisations in the south. Word-final voiced obstruents are generally devoiced. Learn lexical stress and reduced unstressed e (schwa). Dutch speech differs in the Netherlands and Belgium.
building: boek → boekje = book → little book. Diminutives take het: het boekje, even when the original noun uses de. The exact suffix can be -je, -tje, -pje, -etje or -kje.
taal + cursus → taalcursus = language course. The final noun supplies the main meaning and normally its gender.
opbellen = to phone; Ik bel je op. = I phone you. In a subordinate clause: omdat ik je opbel = because I phone you.

sections.title: Gender, articles and adjectives
sections.explanation: Dutch distinguishes common-gender de nouns and neuter het nouns; plurals use de. Diminutives are normally neuter. Attributive adjectives usually take -e, but an indefinite singular neuter noun often has no -e: een goed boek versus het goede boek. Predicative adjectives normally remain uninflected. Lexical and fixed-expression exceptions deserve example-based study.
examples: een interessant boek / het interessante boek
an interesting book / the interesting book
exercises: Complete: een klein__ huis.
Een klein huis. Indefinite singular neuter pattern.
What article do ordinary plurals take?
De: de boeken, de huizen.

sections.title: Verb position and separable verbs
sections.explanation: Main declaratives place the finite verb in second constituent position; a fronted adverb inverts subject and verb. Subordinate clauses often place verb material at the end. Separable verbs split in suitable main clauses: ik bel je op. Infinitives and participles form a sentence bracket; subordinate verb-cluster orders have variation and should be studied from reliable standard examples.
examples: Tomorrow I will discuss the report.
Ik denk dat hij het rapport heeft gelezen.
I think he has read the report.
Embedded clause with final verb cluster.
exercises: Reorder morgen / ik / begin.
Morgen begin ik. Fronting requires the finite verb before the subject.
Use opbellen in a main clause.
Ik bel de collega morgen op. The prefix closes the bracket.

sections.title: Time, passive and modality
sections.explanation: Perfect tense uses hebben or zijn with a participle, with lexical and motion-related patterns. Written narration can favour the simple past. Present tense frequently refers to planned future events. Worden + participle forms an event passive; zijn + participle can express a state or perfect passive depending on context. Zou supports polite and hypothetical meanings; moeten and hoeven differ under negation.
examples: You do not have to wait.
exercises: Contrast niet mogen and niet hoeven.
Niet mogen forbids or denies permission; niet hoeven removes necessity.
Request clarification politely.
Zou u dit punt kunnen toelichten? A conventional courteous question.

sections.title: Relative clauses, er and formal structure
sections.explanation: Die refers to de nouns and dat to singular het nouns in core relative patterns. Relative clauses are verb-final. Er has several functions: location, existence, quantities and pronominal adverbs. Er zijn drie opties introduces existence; ik heb er drie represents a quantity. Combinations such as daarmee and hierover replace preposition + thing relationships; human references can need other forms.
examples: het rapport dat we gisteren hebben ontvangen
Het noun with dat and a final verb cluster.
exercises: Choose de methode die / dat we gebruiken.
Die. Methode is a de noun.
Explain ik heb er twee.
I have two of them. Er carries the understood quantified noun.

sections.title: Professional reading and writing
sections.explanation:
Teaching passage: De resultaten wijzen op een verband tussen twee factoren. Ze bewijzen echter niet dat de ene factor de andere veroorzaakt. Bij de beoordeling van de conclusie moeten de omstandigheden van het onderzoek worden meegenomen.
Translation: The results indicate a relationship between two factors. However, they do not prove that one causes the other. The study conditions must be included when assessing the conclusion. Echter signals contrast; wijzen op is not equivalent to proving. Use u or je according to the relationship, not a rigid claim that every workplace uses formal address.
examples: Kunt u aangeven waarop deze schatting is gebaseerd?
Could you indicate what this estimate is based on?
Professional clarification with a pronominal-adverb relation.
It does not necessarily follow from that that ...
A limited inference, useful in argument.
exercises: Summarise without claiming causation.
The passage reports a relationship, denies proof of a causal direction and asks readers to consider conditions.
Write a professional request in 100 words.
Check verb-second, subordinate clusters, de/het choices and a clear requested action.

rules.title: De and het
rules.explanation: Dutch distinguishes common-gender de nouns and neuter het nouns; plurals use de. Een introduces an indefinite singular noun. Diminutives take het regardless of the base noun’s gender.

examples.native: Mexico-Stad is de hoofdstad van Mexico.
examples.translation: Mexico City is the capital of Mexico.

examples.native: Een vrouwenhater moet je echt zo hard vertrouwen als het weer.
examples.translation: We must trust misogynists as much as we can trust the weather.

examples.native: Ik ben in de keuken.
examples.translation: I'm in the kitchen.

rules.title: Demonstratives
rules.explanation: Dit/dat commonly pair with singular het nouns; deze/die with de nouns and plurals. Distance and discourse determine the near/far distinction.

examples.native: Dit boek was gemakkelijk.
examples.translation: This book was easy.

examples.native: Ik heb geen idee hoe ze dat voor elkaar gekregen hebben.
examples.translation: I don't know how they did it.

examples.native: Wie heeft je dit aangedaan?
examples.translation: Who did this to you?

rules.title: Personal pronouns
rules.explanation: Dutch pronouns have stressed and unstressed forms. Je/ze/we are common reduced forms. U is polite you and follows its own agreement patterns.

examples.native: Jullie zijn goud waard.
examples.translation: You're worth gold.

examples.native: Ik ga vandaag niet meer werken.
examples.translation: I am not going to work more today.

examples.native: Hoelang moeten we wachten, denk je?
examples.translation: How long do you think we'll have to wait?

rules.title: Zijn forms
rules.explanation: Zijn is irregular. Main statements normally place the finite verb second; yes/no questions place it first. With jij/je after the verb, the present -t is often absent in applicable verbs.

examples.native: Mijn Frans is nog steeds niet zo goed.
examples.translation: My French is still not very good.

examples.native: Sommige mensen zijn allergisch voor latex.
examples.translation: Some people are allergic to latex.

examples.native: Alles is helder.
examples.translation: Everything is clear.

rules.title: Hebben forms
rules.explanation: Hebben expresses possession and serves as an auxiliary. The finite form agrees with the subject; a participle or infinitive can stand at the end of the clause.

examples.native: Water heeft nul calorieën.
examples.translation: Water has zero calories.

examples.native: Tom heeft hoop.
examples.translation: Tom has hope.

examples.native: Toms huis heeft een kleine keuken.
examples.translation: Tom's house has a tiny kitchen.

rules.title: Subordinate connectors
rules.explanation: Subordinate clauses usually put their verb cluster late. Of can introduce an indirect yes/no question. An ordinary main clause follows verb-second order.

examples.native: Als het weer gebeurt, laat het me meteen weten a.u.b.
examples.translation: If it happens again, please let me know right away.

examples.native: Jeff was drie maanden op zoek voordat hij een baan vond.
examples.translation: Jeff searched for three months before he found a job.

examples.native: De motor stopt als je op die knop drukt.
examples.translation: If you pressed that button, the engine would stop.

rules.title: Negation
rules.explanation: Geen negates many indefinite noun phrases; niet negates a predicate or other constituent. Niet placement controls which part is negated.

examples.native: Om het even wat ze eet, ze verdikt niet.
examples.translation: However much she eats, she never gains weight.

examples.native: Ik wil niet slapen.
examples.translation: I don't want to sleep.

examples.native: Hij is duidelijk niet zo'n soort persoon.
examples.translation: Obviously, he's not that kind of person.

rules.title: Modal verbs
rules.explanation: Modals govern an infinitive and express ability, obligation, permission, desire or prediction. The finite modal occupies the normal finite-verb position; the infinitive commonly stands late.

examples.native: De tijd zal het zeggen.
examples.translation: Time will tell.

examples.native: Ja, ik kan.
examples.translation: Yes, I can.

examples.native: Wat wil je?
examples.translation: What do you want?

rules.title: Past zijn and hebben
rules.explanation: Was/waren and had/hadden are common past forms. They can be main verbs or auxiliaries; a later participle determines whether a pluperfect construction is present.

examples.native: De Romeinse troepen waren uitgeput.
examples.translation: The Roman troops were exhausted.

examples.native: Hoe was je biologie-examen?
examples.translation: How was your biology exam?

examples.native: Ik was zeer trots.
examples.translation: I was very proud.

rules.title: Past participles
rules.explanation: A perfect combines hebben or zijn with a past participle. Motion/change verbs may use zijn in relevant meanings; learn auxiliary choice with the verb.

examples.native: Wie heeft die doos gemaakt?
examples.translation: Who made this box?

examples.native: Het maakt niet uit wat ze gezegd heeft.
examples.translation: It doesn't matter what she said.

examples.native: Ik ben nooit in het buitenland geweest.
examples.translation: I've never been abroad.

rules.title: Conditional forms
rules.explanation: Zou/zouden often mark a conditional or future in the past. Kon/konden can be past ability or hypothetical ability. Context determines whether the situation is factual or unreal.

examples.native: Ik wou dat ik kon stoppen met denken aan Tom.
examples.translation: I wish I could stop thinking about Tom.

examples.native: Als ik het alfabet kon herschikken, dan zette ik nog steeds T voor U.
examples.translation: If I could rearrange the alphabet, I would put U and I together.

examples.native: Ik wist wel dat Tom dorst zou hebben.
examples.translation: I knew Tom would be thirsty.

rules.title: Passives and worden
rules.explanation: Worden plus participle commonly forms an event passive. Worden can also mean become. Inspect the complete predicate before naming the construction.

examples.native: Die hierboven vermelde zending werd behoorlijk afgeleverd.
examples.translation: The above-mentioned mail item has been duly delivered.

examples.native: Frans wordt gesproken in Zwitserland.
examples.translation: French is spoken in Switzerland.

examples.native: Het Catalaans wordt gesproken in Andorra.
examples.translation: Catalan is spoken in Andorra.

rules.title: Relative pronouns
rules.explanation: Die generally relates to de nouns and plurals; dat to singular het nouns. Wie/wat occur in other relative and interrogative constructions. The relative clause has subordinate word order.

examples.native: Alle zinnen die we verzamelen geven we uit onder de licentie Creatieve Commons - Naamsvermelding.
examples.translation: We're releasing all the sentences we collect under the Creative Commons Attribution license.

examples.native: Wat is je meest geliefde vakantiebestemming?
examples.translation: What's your favorite vacation place?

examples.native: Van wie zijn de sleutels?
examples.translation: Who do the keys belong to?

rules.title: Er in context
rules.explanation: Er can express a location, introduce an existence statement, support a quantity or occur in a pronominal adverb. Analyse its actual construction instead of assigning one English equivalent.

examples.native: De oude man zag er wijs uit.
examples.translation: The old man looked wise.

examples.native: Er zijn veel dieren te zien in dit bos.
examples.translation: You can see many animals in this forest.

examples.native: Er zijn veel boeken in mijn kamer.
examples.translation: There are many books in my room.

rules.title: Infinitives and purpose
rules.explanation: Many infinitive complements use te; om ... te commonly expresses purpose. Te can also intensify an adjective, so identify the following phrase.

examples.native: Ze ging op haar knieën om te bidden.
examples.translation: She went down on her knees to pray.

examples.native: Tom zat op de bank te roken.
examples.translation: Tom sat on the bench smoking.

examples.native: Tom rijdt altijd te hard.
examples.translation: Tom always drives too fast.

rules.title: Adjectives
rules.explanation: Attributive adjectives often take -e. An indefinite singular neuter noun often has an uninflected adjective: een goed boek. A predicative adjective normally has no -e.

examples.native: Ik woon in een heel klein appartement.
examples.translation: I live in a very small apartment.

examples.native: Dit is goed vlees.
examples.translation: This is good meat.

examples.native: Luxemburg is een klein land.
examples.translation: Luxembourg is a small country.

rules.title: Coordination
rules.explanation: Coordinating conjunctions connect similar structures without imposing subordinate verb-final order. Want supplies a reason with main-clause grammar.

examples.native: Tom en Maria zijn aan het liften.
examples.translation: Tom and Mary are hitchhiking.

examples.native: Hij is jong, maar wel heel intelligent.
examples.translation: He's young, but he's very intelligent.

examples.native: Ze exporteren veel fruit, zoals sinaasappels, grapefruits en citroenen.
examples.translation: They export a lot of fruit, such as oranges, grapefruits and lemons.

rules.title: Questions
rules.explanation: A direct question often places the finite verb before the subject. An indirect question introduced by a question word normally follows subordinate order.

examples.native: Waar is jullie zoon?
examples.translation: Where's your son?

examples.native: Waar is uw huiswerk?
examples.translation: Where is your homework?

examples.native: Waar ben je nu op dit moment?
examples.translation: Where are you right now?

rules.title: Comparison
rules.explanation: Comparatives commonly use dan; equality commonly uses zo ... als. Beter is the irregular comparative of goed. Distinguish comparison from other uses of dan/als.

examples.native: In alle geval kunt ge beter gehoorzamen aan uw ouders.
examples.translation: In any case you had better obey your parents.

examples.native: Ze is twee jaar ouder dan jij.
examples.translation: She is two years older than you.

examples.native: De school is verder dan het station.
examples.translation: The school is farther than the station.

rules.title: Cause and concession
rules.explanation: Hoewel introduces concession in a subordinate clause. Daarom and dus express a consequence; toch and echter can signal contrast. Linking meaning and word order need separate attention.

examples.native: Daarom hou ik van je.
examples.translation: That's why I like you.

examples.native: Het ziet ernaar uit dat de wereld toch niet is vergaan op 21 december.
examples.translation: It looks like the world didn't end on December 21st after all.

examples.native: Ik ben gay, dus?
examples.translation: I'm gay, so?

passages.title: Learning with a clear purpose
passages.native: Ik leer een nieuwe taal. Elke dag lees ik een korte tekst en luister ik naar duidelijke voorbeelden. Ik schrijf nuttige woorden in een schrift. Wanneer ik een fout maak, bekijk ik de regel en probeer ik het opnieuw. Mijn doel is mensen te begrijpen en mijn gedachten duidelijk uit te drukken.
passages.translation: I am learning a new language. Each day, I read a short text and listen to clear examples. I write useful words in a notebook. When I make a mistake, I check the rule and try again. My goal is to understand people and express my ideas clearly.

grammarTerms: Noun
A word naming a person, thing or idea: student, book, freedom.
Verb
A word describing an action or state: read, know, be.
Subject
The participant linked to the main verb’s subject pattern. In The student reads a book, the student is the subject.
Object
A participant selected by a verb. In The student reads a book, a book is the direct object.
Agreement
One word changes to match another, for example an adjective matching a noun’s gender and number.
Case
A noun/pronoun form marking its relationship in a sentence. Cases can mark subjects, objects, possession or relations usually expressed by English prepositions.
Gender
A grammatical noun class. It does not always describe the sex of a person or any physical property.
Tense
A verb system that relates a situation to a time, often past or non-past.
Aspect
How a situation is viewed: unfolding, completed, habitual, experienced or in a resulting state.
Infinitive
A non-finite verb form often used for a dictionary entry or a complement. It does not by itself give the ordinary person/tense pattern.
Participle
A verb-derived form used in compound predicates or as a modifier; its exact function depends on the language and construction.
Clause
A unit organised around a predicate. One sentence can contain several clauses.
Register
Language choices suited to a situation: casual conversation, polite requests, academic writing or another context.
